questions.q: In terms of the graph of average binding energy per nucleon against mass number, why does splitting a large nucleus such as uranium release energy?
options: The two fission fragments have a lower average binding energy per nucleon than the original nucleus
Splitting a large mass number nucleus in two produces nuclei with a higher average binding energy per nucleon than the original nucleus, so energy is released
The fragments move further from iron-56, the most stable nucleus, releasing the difference in mass
Uranium sits at the peak of the curve, so any change in mass number releases energy
questions.explanation: Page 413 states that taking a large mass number nucleus and splitting it in two produces nuclei with a higher average binding energy per nucleon than the original, so energy is released. The most stable nuclei have a mass number of about 50 to 60, with iron-56 the most stable, so the fragments climb toward that peak.

questions.q: Meitner and Frisch calculated that the fission of one uranium-235 nucleus produces about 200 MeV of energy. In what form does most of this energy appear, and how does it compare with burning coal?
options: Mostly as gamma radiation; about the same energy per atom as burning carbon in coal
Mainly as kinetic energy of the fission fragments; about 20 million times more energy than the 10 eV released per carbon atom burned in coal
Mainly as the binding energy of the emitted neutrons; about 200 times more than burning coal
Mostly as heat in the surrounding water; roughly twice the energy released per carbon atom in coal
questions.explanation: Page 421 records that the fission of one uranium-235 nucleus produces about 200 MeV, mainly as kinetic energy of the fission fragments. Each carbon atom burned in coal releases only about 10 eV, so fission releases roughly 20 million times more energy per atom.

questions.q: Joliot's team confirmed in 1939 that each fission reaction of uranium-235 emits two or three fast neutrons. Why was this result so significant?
options: It proved that uranium-235 decays only by alpha emission
It showed that the emitted neutrons could go on to cause further fissions, allowing the possibility of a chain reaction that releases enormous amounts of energy
It demonstrated that fission fragments are always barium and krypton
It confirmed that neutrons carry an electric charge of +1
questions.explanation: Page 421 explains that two or three fast neutrons emitted with each fission reaction allowed for the possibility of a chain reaction, which could potentially release enormous amounts of energy. Each released neutron can be captured by another uranium-235 nucleus and trigger a further fission.

questions.q: A neutron emitted when a uranium-235 nucleus undergoes fission may have an energy of about 1 MeV. What is the approximate energy of a 'thermal' neutron of the kind that would be captured by a uranium-235 nucleus in a nuclear reactor?
options: About 1 MeV — the same as the neutron just emitted
About 0.02 MeV — a much slower, thermal neutron
About 200 MeV — equal to the energy of the whole fission
About 10 eV — the same as a carbon atom burned in coal
questions.explanation: Page 400 states that a neutron emitted in fission may have an energy of about 1 MeV, while a thermal neutron that would be captured by a uranium-235 nucleus in a nuclear reactor has an energy of about 0.02 MeV. Slow, thermal neutrons are far more readily captured than the fast ones born in fission, which is why a reactor needs a moderator.

questions.q: A possible fission reaction is \(^{235}_{92}\mathrm{U} + ^{1}_{0}n \rightarrow ^{139}_{57}\mathrm{La} + ^{95}_{42}\mathrm{Mo} + 2(^{1}_{0}n) + 7(^{0}_{-1}e)\). Using the atomic masses below, find the energy released (in MeV) when one uranium-235 nucleus undergoes this fission.
questions.explanation: The energy released equals the energy equivalent of the decrease in mass. Since the products have less mass than the reactants, that mass difference (0.3196 u) is converted to energy using \(1\,\mathrm{u} = 931.5\,\mathrm{MeV}\), giving 297.7 MeV per fission.

questions.q: Uranium-235 absorbs a neutron and undergoes fission producing barium-141, krypton-92 and some neutrons: \(^{235}_{92}\mathrm{U} + ^{1}_{0}n \rightarrow ^{141}_{56}\mathrm{Ba} + ^{92}_{36}\mathrm{Kr} + x\,^{1}_{0}n\). How many neutrons are released?
questions.given: Mass numbers must balance: left side \(235 + 1\); right side \(141 + 92 + x\). Atomic numbers must balance: left \(92\); right \(56 + 36\).
working: Balance the mass numbers (top): \(235 + 1 = 236\) on the left
Check atomic numbers (bottom): \(56 + 36 = 92\), and the neutrons add zero charge — balanced
questions.explanation: Every nuclear equation must conserve mass number and atomic number. The mass numbers give 236 = 141 + 92 + 3, so three neutrons are released, and the charges balance with 92 = 56 + 36. This is one of the standard uranium-235 fission equations on page 421.

questions.q: From memory: what does the graph of average binding energy per nucleon against mass number tell us about which nuclei are most stable, and why this means both fusion and fission can release energy?
keyPoints: The most stable nuclei have a mass number of about 50 to 60; the most stable nucleus is iron-56, at the peak of the curve.
Joining light nuclei produces nuclei with a higher average binding energy per nucleon, releasing energy — this is nuclear fusion.
Splitting a large mass number nucleus in two also produces nuclei with a higher average binding energy per nucleon, releasing energy — this is nuclear fission.
questions.explanation: If you recalled that iron-56 (mass number about 50 to 60) is the most stable nucleus, and that moving toward it from either end of the curve raises the average binding energy per nucleon and releases energy, grade yourself Good or Easy.

questions.q: In a nuclear reactor, what is the key difference between the job of the moderator and the job of the control rods?
options: The moderator absorbs neutrons to slow the reaction; the control rods slow neutrons to sustain it
The moderator (e.g. water or graphite) slows fast neutrons so they are more readily captured; the control rods (e.g. cadmium or boron) absorb neutrons to set the reaction rate
Both absorb neutrons, but the moderator does it faster
The moderator cools the core while the control rods provide the fissile fuel
questions.explanation: Swapping these two is the most common mark-loser in this topic. The moderator slows fast neutrons to thermal speeds so they are more likely to be captured and cause fission; the control rods absorb neutrons, removing them from the chain — inserting them further slows the reaction, withdrawing them speeds it up.

questions.q: Name the four main components of a nuclear fission reactor and state the one-word job of each (use the episode's mnemonic).
keyPoints: Fast Cars Make Crashes: Fuel, Control rods, Moderator, Coolant.
Fuel provides — the enriched uranium supplies the fissile uranium-235 nuclei, energy and neutrons.
Control rods absorb — cadmium or boron rods absorb neutrons to set the reaction rate.
Moderator slows — water or graphite slows fast neutrons so they are captured; Coolant cools — carries heat away to make steam and prevent meltdown.
questions.explanation: Marks here come from pairing each component with its mechanism (provide, absorb, slow, cool), not just naming it. If you got all four parts and their jobs, grade Good or Easy.

questions.q: Describe the structure and function of a nuclear fission reactor, naming each major component and stating what it does. (6 marks)
questions.modelAnswer: A nuclear fission reactor has four main components. The fuel, usually enriched uranium containing uranium-235, provides the fissile nuclei that undergo fission, releasing energy and neutrons. The control rods, made of a neutron-absorbing material such as cadmium or boron, absorb neutrons; inserting them further into the core absorbs more neutrons and slows the reaction, while withdrawing them speeds it up, holding the chain reaction at a steady rate of one further fission per fission. The moderator, such as water or graphite, slows the fast neutrons released by fission to thermal speeds, making them more likely to be captured and cause further fission, sustaining the chain reaction. The coolant, often water, carries the heat generated in the core away to a heat exchanger to produce steam that drives turbines for electricity, and prevents the core from overheating.

criteria.descriptor: Fuel: enriched uranium provides the fissile nuclei, energy and neutrons.
Control rods: absorb neutrons (cadmium/boron) to set the reaction rate.
Moderator: slows fast neutrons to thermal speeds to sustain the chain reaction.
Coolant: removes heat to generate steam/electricity and prevent overheating.
Each component is paired with its function (mechanism stated, not just named).
Links components to holding a controlled chain reaction at one fission per fission.

questions.explanation: A band-six answer states what each part is made of and the mechanism by which it works (control rods absorb, moderator slows), not just a label. The mnemonic Fast Cars Make Crashes locks the four parts: Fuel provides, Control rods absorb, Moderator slows, Coolant cools.
